doc.title: George Russell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
title: Arranging for Ventura, Shaw and Thornhill; Gil Evans's gift for color
summary: Asked about arranging for Charlie Ventura, Artie Shaw and Claude Thornhill, Russell contrasts his melodic focus with Gil Evans's orchestral color.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: The healing feeling. We talked earlier, and I’m sort of going back to it a little bit – we’re going to of course talk extensively about The Lydian. You’re going to talking about The Lydian. I’m not going to sit here with the master and try to talk about The Lydian. But . . .
Well, the master may not be able to convey anything to you about it.

I think you’ll elucidate a lot for us. I read somewhere – I don’t remember what the source was – that you had arranged some songs for Charlie Ventura, for Artie Shaw, for Claude Thornhill. I remember thinking at one point – and please correctly me if I’m wrong, and I probably am – I remember thinking at one point, oh those were probably just paying gigs. But then, Claude Thornhill made some interesting music.
I’m thinking now, probably one of the reasons I was attracted to his music was because you were – had a hand not only in a lot of the specific pieces, but probably helped open up his thinking.
That’s Gil Evans. Gil is completely, I think – I think he opened Claude up, although Claude was already – had a style. I think that style Gil enriched.

With his arranging talents. Was that immediately – when you were writing those songs, was that sort of around the same time – just prior to you – I hate to deal with this in a linear fashion, but I’m just trying to get the question out. Where was that in relation to when you hooked up with Dizzy and you guys were doing Symphony Hall?

I don’t know if I ever – Gil was a master of color, of taking chords and using them as colors. I wasn’t – I was probably more concerned about the type of melody I would have. I wasn’t – when you think of Gil, you see colors, because that’s what he was good at. His orchestration is absolutely beautiful, because he cares about orchestration. So I wasn’t advanced enough to have his orchestrational gifts. That’s what it really was.
Also, he was a man who had the art of – seeing life through his eyes was a very beautiful thing. He’s a beautiful man. That’s all I can say.
